Lessons.Title: Explain Equivalence
ExplanationParagraphs: Grade4 Unit2 Lesson9 Explain Equivalence (Illustrative Mathematics K–5 First Edition 2021). Retain existing learning goals and curriculum identifiers: show two rational shares refer to same point on a number line and justify conceptually using unit parts.
Warm-up 10min Number Talk: 10×6=60,10×12=120,10×24=240,5×24=120. Record the related doubling and halving multiplication strategies with partner discussion.

Activity1 Pointed Discussion 20min. Andre, Lin and Clare consider 70/100 on a number line. Andre thinks100 partitions are necessary. Lin recommends7/10: yes, equals70/100 at the same point. Clare recommends3/5: no, equals60/100, a different location. Explain with related-sized fractional parts and revise explanation after partner feedback, MLR1 Stronger and Clearer Each Time.

Activity2 How Do You Know 15min. Groups3–4 get4 sticky notes and visit ≥2 of six original teacher posters, including at least one A–C and one D–F. For A–C show the two existing fractions equivalent and add a NEW equivalent fraction. For D–F select exactly the two equivalent fractions and explain why the remaining value is NOT equal. This is a teacher-managed gallery, not an automatically checked multiple-choice substitute.

Teacher poster original source groups: A2/10 and20/100; B6/4 and18/12; C3/5 and60/100; D1/4,3/12,30/100; E15/6,7/4,30/12; F7/3,21/10,28/12. D equivalent pair1/4=3/12, E15/6=30/12, F7/3=28/12. Other three fractions are deliberate counterexamples, never classify the entire triple as equivalent.

Lesson synthesis 10min: compare equality of unit sizes, partition counts, and positions on the same number line. Explain why dividing whole into100 equal parts is not always necessary; invite reasoned feedback.

Edulytics independently authored five-minute Cool-down, NOT original publisher gated prompt: Explain why70/100=7/10 but70/100≠3/5; on poster D identify exactly the equivalent pair and show a number-line or equivalent-part explanation. Teacher assesses argument; existing numerical Practice assesses only exact equivalence.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fractions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different names for the same rational quantity and same point on the same unit-length number line.
KeyConcepts.Rule: a/b=c/d iff a×d=c×b; explain conceptually using parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Non-equivalence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two fractions at distinct number-line locations, even when numerators and denominators seem related.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Refute with a unit-size argument or exact comparison.

KeyConcepts.Title: Peer explanation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use diagrams or oral/written reasoning to defend/refute a claim.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Three-item source posters deliberately contain one non-equivalent fraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Lin and Clare
WorkedExamples.Question: Which of7/10 or3/5 equals70/100?
Steps: 7/10=70/100 by dividing each tenth into10 hundredths.
3/5=60/100 by dividing each fifth into20 hundredths.
Therefore Lin agrees with70/100; Clare does not.

WorkedExamples.Title: Poster E
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the equivalent pair among15/6,7/4,30/12.
WorkedExamples.Method: Reason with fractional shares or reduce.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent exact fraction reasoning
WorkedExamples.Question: Decide whether 3/5 equals 60/100.
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert to equivalent equal-sized fractional parts and check the comparison.
Steps: Scale numerator and denominator of 3/5 by 20.
Both fractions therefore name the same portion of one whole.
WorkedExamples.Check: First-party mathematical calculation; original pupil diagrams and open reasoning require separate teacher review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling all three fractions on original poster D, E or F equivalent.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Each triple deliberately contains a distractor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare fractions pairwise and justify the one genuinely equal pair.
Use equal whole number-line partitions, not similarity of digits.
